lessons.title: Relevance, Preliminary Questions and Limiting Instructions
body: Evidence law begins with a gateway. Under Federal Rule of Evidence 401, evidence is relevant if it has any tendency to make a fact more or less probable than it would be without the evidence, and the fact is of consequence in determining the action. Rule 402 then says relevant evidence is admissible unless the Constitution, a federal statute, the Rules or other rules prescribed by the Supreme Court provide otherwise, and irrelevant evidence is not admissible. The test is deliberately generous. Relevance is not sufficiency: a single piece of proof need not establish a point, only nudge the probabilities. A fact "of consequence" is one that matters under the substantive law, so the elements of the claim and defenses define what counts, and facts bearing on a witness's credibility also qualify.

Relevance is often described as two linked ideas, probative value (the strength of the inference) and materiality (whether the fact matters under the governing law). Evidence that the defendant in a negligence suit owned a red car is immaterial if color has no bearing on any claim. Evidence that he was seen drinking an hour before the crash is both material and probative on breach.

Preliminary questions are handled by Rule 104. Under Rule 104(a), the judge decides questions of admissibility, such as whether a witness is qualified, a privilege exists or a hearsay exception applies. In making those findings the judge is not bound by the rules of evidence except those on privilege, and applies a preponderance standard (Bourjaily v. United States, 1987). Rule 104(b) is different. When relevance depends on whether another fact exists, the proponent must introduce evidence sufficient to support a finding of that fact, and the jury ultimately decides it. This is conditional relevance. A letter is relevant to show notice only if the defendant actually received it; the judge asks only whether a reasonable jury could find receipt, not whether she herself finds it so.

Rule 105 governs evidence admissible for one purpose or against one party but not another. On request, the court must restrict the evidence to its proper scope and instruct the jury accordingly. A limiting instruction is a cure many lawyers distrust, yet in most settings it is the law's answer, with the exception of a few situations, such as a nontestifying codefendant's confession naming the defendant, where the Supreme Court has found instructions inadequate (Bruton v. United States, 1968).

Worked example. In a contract suit, the plaintiff offers an email the defendant allegedly wrote. The email is plainly relevant if the defendant wrote it. The judge treats authorship as a 104(b) question: if the plaintiff offers enough proof that a jury could find the defendant wrote it (for example, the account, the signature block and a reply that references it), the email goes to the jury, and the defendant may argue it is a forgery. If the same email is admissible only against one of two co-defendants, the other defendant may ask for a limiting instruction.

lessons.title: Rule 403 and Old Chief
body: Rule 403 is the great safety valve. It states that the court may exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by a danger of unfair prejudice, confusing the issues, misleading the jury, undue delay, wasting time or needlessly presenting cumulative evidence. Several features matter. The rule is permissive ("may exclude"), the balance is tilted toward admission because probative value must be substantially outweighed, and the judge has wide discretion, which appellate courts review only for abuse.

The key word is unfair. All good evidence prejudices the opponent; that is what evidence does. Unfair prejudice means an undue tendency to suggest decision on an improper basis, commonly an emotional one, or to lead the jury to punish a party for something other than the charged conduct. Graphic photographs, for example, are routinely admitted when they help prove cause of death or intent, and excluded when they only inflame and the point is undisputed. Confusion and misleading the jury concern mini-trials on collateral matters. Delay and waste are efficiency concerns.

Probative value is not assessed in a vacuum. In Old Chief v. United States (1997), the defendant was charged with being a felon in possession of a firearm; the prior felony was an element of the crime, but the particular nature of the earlier offense (assault causing serious bodily injury) added to the risk of unfair prejudice because the jury might infer a violent disposition. He offered to stipulate that he had a qualifying conviction. The Supreme Court held that the district court abused its discretion in rejecting the stipulation, because the name and nature of the prior offense had little added probative value given the availability of a conclusive stipulation, and the risk of unfair prejudice was substantial. The Court stressed that this is a limited holding. As a general rule, the prosecution may prove its case by evidence of its own choosing, and a defendant cannot ordinarily force it to accept a stipulation in place of live proof, because a story told with narrative force is part of the government's legitimate case.

Trap: Old Chief does not mean a stipulation always defeats admission. It turns on an element the stipulation entirely satisfies, with an offense name that carries an independent prejudicial charge. It is also not a rule of exclusion of prior convictions generally; other rules (404, 609) address those.

Worked example. In a civil battery case, the plaintiff offers twenty-five nearly identical photographs of her bruising. The first two are probative; the remaining twenty-three are cumulative and some are graphic. The judge may admit a few and exclude the rest under 403 for needless presentation of cumulative evidence. A court that excludes all of them would be on weaker ground, because the injuries are a fact of consequence and the photographs are strong proof.

lessons.title: Character Evidence: The Propensity Ban
body: The character rule, Rule 404(a)(1), says evidence of a person's character or character trait is not admissible to prove that on a particular occasion the person acted in accordance with it. This is the propensity ban. The fear is that juries will overvalue a bad history and punish the person for who she is, or decide a case on the basis of a generalization that does not fit the occasion.

The ban has exceptions, and they are the core of exam questions. In a criminal case, the accused may offer evidence of a pertinent trait of character (such as honesty in a fraud case, or peacefulness in an assault case), which opens the door for the prosecutor to rebut it. The accused may also offer evidence of a pertinent trait of the alleged victim, and if he does, the prosecutor may offer evidence of the same trait of the accused. If the defendant in a homicide case says the victim was the first aggressor, the prosecutor may offer evidence of the victim's peacefulness. Only the accused starts this process; the prosecution may not initiate attacks on the accused's character in its case in chief. The third exception is witness character, governed by the impeachment rules (607 to 609). In civil cases there is no general door-opening exception, and character is usually inadmissible when offered as circumstantial proof of conduct.

Rule 405 governs the method of proof. When character evidence is allowed, it may be proved by testimony about reputation or by testimony in the form of an opinion. On cross-examination of the character witness, the court may allow inquiry into relevant specific instances of the person's conduct. In the classic Michelson v. United States (1948), a defendant charged with bribery called character witnesses to his good reputation; on cross, the prosecutor asked whether they had heard of his earlier arrest. The Supreme Court allowed the inquiry, reasoning that the question tests the witness's knowledge and standards, and the court gives a limiting instruction. Counsel must have a good faith basis for the question, and the form "have you heard" is traditionally used for reputation witnesses, while "did you know" is used for opinion witnesses.

When character is itself an essential element of a charge, claim or defense, such as defamation where truth of a character allegation is the defense, or negligent entrustment and child-custody cases, it can be proved by specific instances as well. Here character is not used to infer conduct; it is the thing being decided.

Worked example. D is charged with assault after a bar fight. D calls a friend who testifies that D is a peaceful person. The friend has just opened the door. On cross, the prosecutor may ask, "Did you know that D was arrested for punching a coworker last year?" The question is allowed to test the witness, not to prove D punched anyone. If D had said nothing about his own character, the prosecutor could not have introduced the arrest to prove D is violent.

lessons.title: Other Acts, Habit and the Policy Exclusions
body: Rule 404(b) has two halves. The first forbids using evidence of a crime, wrong or other act to prove a person's character in order to show action in accordance with it. The second permits that same evidence for another purpose, such as proving motive, opportunity, intent, preparation, plan, knowledge, identity, absence of mistake or lack of accident. The list is illustrative, not exclusive. The key is a chain of reasoning that does not pass through propensity. For example, a burglar's earlier use of a distinctive method may identify him (signature or modus operandi), and a prior similar act may rebut the claim that a fatal poisoning was an accident. In a criminal case the prosecutor must provide reasonable notice in writing before trial if the defendant asks for it. Under Huddleston v. United States (1988), the court need not find by a preponderance that the other act occurred; it is a 104(b) question, and the evidence is admissible if a jury could reasonably find the act occurred, though it remains subject to 403.

Rules 413 to 415 create a statutory exception: in sexual assault and child molestation cases, evidence of the defendant's other similar offenses may be admitted and considered for any relevant matter, including propensity, subject to 403.

Habit under Rule 406 differs from character. Evidence of a person's habit or an organization's routine practice may be admitted to prove that on a particular occasion the person or organization acted in accordance with it. Habit is a regular response to a repeated specific situation, such as always signaling at a particular intersection; a general disposition for carefulness is character, not habit. The rule does not require corroboration or an eyewitness.

The policy exclusions share one idea: the evidence may be relevant but is excluded in order to promote some social goal, and it is admissible for other purposes. Rule 407 bars evidence of subsequent remedial measures to prove negligence, culpable conduct, a defect or a need for a warning, in order to encourage safety repairs; it is admissible for another purpose such as ownership, control, impeachment, or feasibility of precautions if the defendant disputes feasibility. Rule 408 bars offers to compromise and statements in negotiations to prove or disprove the validity or amount of a disputed claim, with a dispute required. Rule 409 covers offers to pay medical expenses. Rule 410 protects withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo contendere pleas and statements made during plea discussions with a prosecuting attorney. Rule 411 bars liability insurance evidence on whether a person acted negligently, but permits it to show bias, agency, ownership or control. Rule 412 is the rape shield rule: in a sex offense case, evidence offered to prove a victim's other sexual behavior or sexual predisposition is generally inadmissible, subject to limited criminal exceptions for source of semen or injury, past consent with the accused, and evidence the Constitution requires.

Worked example. After a customer slips in a store, the store installs non-slip mats. The plaintiff cannot use the mats to prove the store was negligent. If the store claims it does not own the area, however, the mats may be admitted to show control.

lessons.title: Defining Hearsay and Spotting Non-Hearsay Uses
body: Hearsay is the most tested subject in evidence law, and the surest way to handle it is to work through the definition step by step. Under Rule 801(c), hearsay is a statement that the declarant does not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing, and that a party offers in evidence to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement. Rule 802 then says hearsay is not admissible unless a federal statute, the Rules or other rules prescribed by the Supreme Court provide otherwise. The rationale is that an out-of-court statement lacks the safeguards of the oath, the witness's presence before the factfinder, and cross-examination, which probes the four hearsay dangers: faulty perception, faulty memory, ambiguity and insincerity.

A statement under Rule 801(a) is a person's oral assertion, written assertion, or nonverbal conduct if the person intended it as an assertion. A nod in response to "Did you see him?" is a statement. Conduct that is not meant to communicate anything, such as a person opening an umbrella, is not a statement under the federal rules, which treat nonassertive conduct as outside the hearsay definition even if a jury would infer a belief from it. A declarant is the person who made the statement, and animals and machines are not declarants; a radar gun reading or a computer-generated timestamp raises authentication, not hearsay.

The key analytical move is to ask what the statement is offered to prove. If the proponent needs the statement to be true to make it relevant, it is hearsay. If the statement is relevant simply because it was made, it is not. Common non-hearsay uses include: the effect on the listener (a warning that the stairs were icy, offered to show the defendant was on notice); verbal acts or legally operative words (the words of a contract offer, a defamatory statement, a bribe offer); circumstantial evidence of the declarant's state of mind, where the statement is relevant whether true or false; and impeachment by a prior inconsistent statement, offered only to show that the witness said something different. Statements offered to show the speaker's knowledge of a fact, to show that the speaker was conscious, or to show a person's language skills, also do not depend on truth.

Trap: the same words can be hearsay for one purpose and non-hearsay for another, and the examiner will often change only the purpose. A declarant's own statement of a future intent ("I'm going to Denver with Walt") is offered under the state-of-mind exception 803(3) to prove the declarant's later conduct, which Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Hillmon (1892) accepted, but it generally is not allowed to prove what another person did.

Worked example. In a premises-liability case, a witness testifies that a neighbor shouted, "The railing is loose!" two days before the plaintiff fell. If offered to show the railing was loose, it is hearsay. If offered to show the landlord, who overheard, knew about the danger, it is not hearsay because the point is notice, and the truth of the statement does not matter.

lessons.title: Statements That Are Not Hearsay: Rule 801(d)
body: Rule 801(d) lists statements that fit the definition of hearsay but are defined as not hearsay. They are called exemptions, and they differ from exceptions in that they are not hearsay by definition, so the declarant's availability and the exact trustworthiness rationale matter less. They fall into two families.

Rule 801(d)(1) covers certain prior statements of a testifying witness. The declarant must testify and be subject to cross-examination about the statement. Then three kinds are exempt. (A) A prior inconsistent statement, but only if given under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, other proceeding, or in a deposition. A casual out-of-court remark to a police officer usually does not qualify, though it may still impeach. (B) A prior consistent statement, if offered either to rebut an express or implied charge that the declarant recently fabricated it or acted from a recent improper influence or motive, or (since a 2014 amendment) to rehabilitate the declarant's credibility as a witness when attacked on another ground. Under Tome v. United States (1995), the common-law premotive requirement remains for the first type: the statement must predate the alleged motive to fabricate. (C) A statement of identification of a person made after perceiving the person, such as a witness picking out the defendant from a lineup.

Rule 801(d)(2) covers statements offered against an opposing party. These are admissions in the broad sense, and they need not have been against interest when made, nor be based on personal knowledge. The five categories are (A) the party's own statement in either an individual or representative capacity; (B) a statement the party manifested that it adopted or believed to be true, as by silence in circumstances where a reasonable person would deny it (an adoptive admission); (C) a statement by a person the party authorized to make a statement on the subject; (D) a statement by the party's agent or employee on a matter within the scope of that relationship and while it existed; and (E) a statement by a coconspirator of the party during and in furtherance of the conspiracy. The statement itself may be considered in deciding whether the declarant had the authority, the agency or the conspiracy, but it does not by itself establish them. In Bourjaily v. United States (1987), the Court held the preliminary facts are decided by a preponderance of the evidence under Rule 104(a). The rule applies only when the statement is offered against the party, so a party cannot offer her own out-of-court statement under it.

Traps. Statements by a coconspirator made after the conspiracy ended, or mere idle chatter, do not satisfy (E). The agent-statement rule (D) requires scope and timing; the statement of a former employee about past events does not qualify. A party's own statement can be admitted even if the party did not personally know the facts.

Worked example. Dale and Evan plot a burglary. After the plan is set, Evan tells a friend, "Dale will handle the alarm," to recruit him. Offered against Dale, the statement can be used as a coconspirator statement made in furtherance, if the court finds the conspiracy and Dale's participation by a preponderance, using the statement along with other evidence. A statement Evan makes to police after his arrest, describing the plan, was not made in furtherance and is not within (E).

lessons.title: Rule 803: Exceptions That Ignore Availability
body: Rule 803 lists exceptions that apply whether or not the declarant is available as a witness. The theory is that these categories of statements carry circumstantial guarantees of reliability, so the lack of cross-examination matters less. The most tested ones follow.

Present sense impression (803(1)): a statement describing or explaining an event or condition, made while or immediately after the declarant perceived it. Excited utterance (803(2)): a statement relating to a startling event or condition, made while the declarant was under the stress of excitement that it caused. The test for the excited utterance is the declarant's mental state, not strict timing, so it can reach statements made some time after the event, while the present sense impression requires near contemporaneity. Then-existing mental, emotional or physical condition (803(3)): a statement of the declarant's then-existing state of mind (such as motive, intent or plan) or emotional, sensory or physical condition (such as pain), but not a statement of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered or believed, unless it relates to the validity or terms of the declarant's will. "I'm afraid of him" qualifies; "I'm afraid of him because he hit me last week" does not qualify as to the past act.

Statements made for medical diagnosis or treatment (803(4)) cover statements describing medical history, symptoms or their cause, if reasonably pertinent to diagnosis or treatment. The rule applies to statements made to any medical provider and even to statements by a person seeking treatment for another, and not only to doctors. Recorded recollection (803(5)): a record on a matter the witness once knew about but now cannot recall well enough to testify fully and accurately, made or adopted when the matter was fresh, and accurately reflecting the witness's knowledge. It may be read into evidence but received as an exhibit only if offered by an adverse party. Refreshing recollection under Rule 612 is a different device, and the writing is not itself evidence.

Records of a regularly conducted activity (803(6)), the business records exception, require a record of an act, event, condition, opinion or diagnosis, made at or near the time by someone with knowledge, kept in the course of regularly conducted activity of a business, organization or occupation, and making the record was a regular practice of that activity, all shown by the testimony of a custodian or qualified witness or by a certification that complies with Rule 902(11) or (12). The opponent may defeat it by showing that the source of information or the method or circumstances of preparation indicate a lack of trustworthiness. Every layer must itself be within an exception or be non-hearsay: a police report recording a bystander's account has an outsider's statement inside it, and that statement needs its own basis (Rule 805).

Public records (803(8)) include a record or statement of a public office setting out the office's activities, or a matter observed while under a legal duty to report (but not, in a criminal case, a matter observed by law-enforcement personnel), or, in a civil case or against the government in a criminal case, factual findings from a legally authorized investigation, unless the opponent shows a lack of trustworthiness. Other exceptions include learned treatises (803(18)), which can be read into evidence but not received as exhibits and must be established as reliable authority by the expert's admission, another expert, or judicial notice; and judgments of a previous conviction (803(22)) for crimes punishable by death or imprisonment over one year.

Worked example. A hospital worker keys a patient's blood-alcohol result into the chart at the time of the test. A records custodian testifies to the hospital's routine. The chart is admissible under 803(6). A note in the chart, "Patient's wife says he drank all day," is a double-hearsay problem, which the medical-treatment exception may or may not solve, depending on whether the wife's statement was reasonably pertinent to diagnosis.

lessons.title: Rule 804, Rule 807, Double Hearsay and Credibility of Declarants
body: Rule 804 contains exceptions that apply only when the declarant is unavailable. Under Rule 804(a), a declarant is unavailable if she is exempted by a ruling of privilege from testifying, refuses to testify despite a court order, testifies to not remembering the subject matter, cannot be present because of death or a then-existing infirmity, physical or mental illness, or cannot be produced by process or other reasonable means. A declarant is not unavailable if the statement's proponent procured or wrongfully caused the unavailability to prevent the testimony.

The main 804(b) exceptions are these. Former testimony (804(b)(1)): testimony given as a witness at a trial, hearing or deposition, if now offered against a party who had (or, in a civil case, whose predecessor in interest had) an opportunity and similar motive to develop it by direct, cross or redirect examination. Statement under the belief of imminent death (804(b)(2)), the dying declaration: in a civil case or a homicide prosecution, a statement the declarant made while believing death was imminent, about its cause or circumstances. Statement against interest (804(b)(3)): a statement that a reasonable person in the declarant's position would have made only if believing it true because it was so contrary to the declarant's proprietary or pecuniary interest or had so great a tendency to invalidate a claim or expose her to civil or criminal liability, and if offered in a criminal case as one tending to expose the declarant to criminal liability, supported by corroborating circumstances that clearly indicate its trustworthiness. In Williamson v. United States (1994), the Court read the predecessor rule to cover only the individual self-inculpatory remarks, not collateral parts of a narrative that shift blame or are neutral. Forfeiture by wrongdoing (804(b)(6)): a statement offered against a party who wrongfully caused, or acquiesced in wrongfully causing, the declarant's
unavailability, and did so intending that result. That intent requirement also appears in the constitutional rule from Giles v. California (2008).

The residual exception, Rule 807, allows a hearsay statement not covered by 803 or 804 if it is supported by sufficient guarantees of trustworthiness, after considering the totality of circumstances under which it was made and any corroborating evidence, and it is more probative on the point than any other evidence the proponent can obtain through reasonable efforts. Since 2019, the proponent must give the adverse party reasonable written notice before trial or hearing. Courts say it should be used sparingly.

Multiple hearsay is addressed in Rule 805: each part of the combined statements must conform with an exception or exemption. Rule 806 allows the credibility of a hearsay declarant to be attacked and supported as if the declarant had testified, including by inconsistent statements even if made after the statement, and without the need to give the declarant an opportunity to explain.

Trap: dying declarations apply only in civil cases and homicide prosecutions, so a victim's deathbed statement in a robbery case does not qualify, and the statement must be about the cause or circumstances of what the declarant believed was her impending death.

Worked example. At a homicide trial, a witness (Rita) refuses to answer despite a judge's order and is held in contempt. She is unavailable. The prosecutor offers her testimony from the preliminary hearing, at which the defendant's counsel cross-examined her. The testimony qualifies as former testimony because the defense had the opportunity and a similar motive to cross at the earlier hearing. If instead the defendant had threatened Rita to keep her quiet, the forfeiture exception could let in her earlier out-of-court accusation.

lessons.title: Crawford and the Testimonial Hearsay Rule
body: The Sixth Amendment guarantees a criminal defendant the right "to be confronted with the witnesses against him." This is a constitutional rule that sits on top of the hearsay rules. A statement can satisfy a hearsay exception and still be barred by the Confrontation Clause, and the reverse is not usually true, because the Clause concerns a narrower set of statements. It applies only in criminal prosecutions and only against the prosecution's evidence; a defendant offering hearsay is not "confronting" anyone.

For decades, Ohio v. Roberts (1980) let hearsay in if it bore adequate indicia of reliability. Crawford v. Washington (2004) overruled that approach for testimonial statements. The Court held that testimonial out-of-court statements by a witness who does not appear at trial are barred unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine. The facts: police questioned Crawford's wife, Sylvia, after he stabbed a man; she gave a recorded statement that undercut his claim of self-defense. Because spousal privilege kept her off the stand, the prosecution played the recording. The Court held that admitting it violated confrontation, regardless of whether a judge found it reliable. Reliability is not the test for testimonial statements; the Clause demands cross-examination as the way the Constitution tests reliability. Crawford left "testimonial" without a full definition, but its core includes ex parte in-court testimony, affidavits, prior testimony at a preliminary hearing or grand jury, and statements made during police interrogations. If the declarant testifies at trial and is subject to cross-examination, the Clause does not bar admission of the earlier statement.

Two years later, Davis v. Washington (2006) supplied the primary purpose test. Statements made to police in the course of interrogation are nontestimonial when the circumstances objectively indicate that the primary purpose of the interrogation is to enable police assistance to meet an ongoing emergency. They are testimonial when the circumstances objectively indicate there is no such ongoing emergency, and the primary purpose is to establish or prove past events potentially relevant to later criminal prosecution. A 911 call in which the caller reports an assault in progress was nontestimonial; a detailed account to officers after the danger had passed, in the companion case Hammon, was testimonial. Michigan v. Bryant (2011) held that the inquiry is objective, takes into account both the declarant's and the interrogator's purposes, and may find an ongoing emergency even when a gunshot victim had fled and the shooter's whereabouts were unknown, because of the threat to police and the public. Ohio v. Clark (2015) held that a three-year-old's statements to preschool teachers identifying his abuser were nontestimonial, noting that statements to persons other than law enforcement are much less likely to be testimonial.

Forfeiture also applies. In Giles v. California (2008) the Court held that the common-law forfeiture-by-wrongdoing doctrine requires that the defendant have intended to prevent the witness from testifying. A statement that is not testimonial is governed only by the hearsay rules and due process, rather than the Clause.

Worked example. A caller tells a 911 operator, while an assailant is still in the house, "He is breaking down my door; his name is Marcus." The primary purpose is to meet an emergency, so the statement is nontestimonial and the Clause does not bar it, even if the caller does not testify. A recorded station-house interview a day later is testimonial, and if the caller is unavailable and was never cross-examined, the statement cannot come in against the defendant.

lessons.title: Forensic Reports, Experts and Joint Trials
body: Forensic evidence raised the hardest Confrontation Clause questions after Crawford. In Melendez-Diaz v. Massachusetts (2009), the Court held that sworn certificates of analysis from a state laboratory, stating that a substance was cocaine, were testimonial statements and the analysts who prepared them were witnesses subject to confrontation. The Court rejected the idea that scientific results are neutral and immune from cross-examination, noting the risks of error, incompetence and fraud. Bullcoming v. New Mexico (2011) held that a surrogate analyst who did not perform or observe the blood-alcohol test cannot substitute for the analyst who signed the certificate, unless the defendant has had a chance to cross-examine that analyst. The prosecution cannot satisfy the Clause by putting another scientist on the stand who knows the lab's procedures.

What about an expert who relies on someone else's test results to form her own opinion? Federal Rule 703 lets an expert rely on inadmissible facts or data if experts in the field reasonably do, and the expert may disclose them to the jury only when their helpfulness in evaluating the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect. The fractured decision in Williams v. Illinois (2012) produced no majority rationale. In Smith v. Arizona (2024), the Court addressed a substitute expert who conveyed to the jury the statements of an absent analyst as the basis of her opinion. It held that when an expert conveys an absent analyst's statements in support of her opinion, and the statements provide that support only if true, then the statements come in for their truth. If those statements are testimonial, the Clause bars them. The Court rejected the idea that labeling the statements "basis evidence" avoids the problem, and remanded for the state court to decide whether the specific statements were testimonial. The upshot: an expert may testify to her own independent conclusions, but may not act as a conduit for another analyst's testimonial assertions offered for their truth.

Business and public records are generally treated as nontestimonial because they are created for administrative purposes, not to prove a fact at trial. Melendez-Diaz said as much about records kept in the regular course of business, though a record created for litigation, such as a lab report prepared for a prosecution, is another matter.

The other major Confrontation problem is the joint trial. In Bruton v. United States (1968), a codefendant's confession that implicated the defendant was admitted at their joint trial with a limiting instruction that it was admissible only against the confessor. The codefendant did not testify. The Court held that the instruction could not cure the harm and the defendant's confrontation right was violated. Richardson v. Marsh (1987) held that the Clause is not violated if the confession is redacted to remove any reference to the defendant and is accompanied by a limiting instruction, even if other evidence at trial links the defendant to it. Gray v. Maryland (1998) held that a redaction that is obvious, such as replacing the name with "deleted" or a blank, falls on the Bruton side. The Bruton rule applies to nontestifying codefendants' testimonial confessions; a codefendant who testifies and can be cross-examined presents no Bruton problem.

Worked example. At a drug trial, the prosecutor calls a chemist who did not run the test but reviewed the lab file, and asks her to read the original analyst's conclusion and say she agrees. If the original analyst's report is testimonial, the defense's objection under Bullcoming and Smith is strong; the prosecution must call the analyst, or the substitute may only offer her own independent opinion based on facts properly in evidence.

lessons.title: Authentication and Self-Authenticating Evidence
body: Authentication is the requirement that, before an item is admitted, the proponent must produce evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims it is (Rule 901(a)). The standard is low: it is a conditional-relevance question under Rule 104(b), so the judge asks whether a reasonable jury could find authenticity, and the jury ultimately decides. The opponent may still contest genuineness before the jury. Authentication is not an issue of hearsay and is a separate hurdle; a genuine letter can still be hearsay, and a perfectly admissible hearsay exception does not authenticate a forgery.

Rule 901(b) offers a non-exclusive list of methods. Testimony of a witness with knowledge that an item is what it is claimed to be (901(b)(1)) is the simplest: a photographer says the picture fairly and accurately depicts the scene. Nonexpert opinion about handwriting, based on familiarity not acquired for the litigation (901(b)(2)). Comparison by an expert or by the trier of fact with specimens already authenticated (901(b)(3)). Distinctive characteristics and the like, including appearance, contents, substance, internal patterns or other distinctive characteristics, taken together with all the circumstances (901(b)(4)), which is the workhorse for emails, text messages and social media posts, where a reply that references private facts or the use of a known account helps show authorship. Voice identification (901(b)(5)). Telephone conversations (901(b)(6)): evidence that a call was made to the number assigned at the time to a particular person or business, if, for a person, self-identification supports it, or for a business, the call reached the business and concerned business reasonably transacted over the phone. A process or system that produces an accurate result (901(b)(9)), common for computer-generated outputs and some video. Chain of custody for fungible items such as drugs or blood samples is a way of showing identity, and breaks in the chain usually go to weight, not admissibility, unless there is a substantial possibility of tampering.

Rule 902 lists items of evidence that are self-authenticating, so no extrinsic evidence of authenticity is needed as a precondition. Examples include domestic public documents under seal (902(1)); domestic public documents not under seal but signed and certified (902(2)); certified copies of public records (902(4)); official publications (902(5)); newspapers and periodicals (902(6)); trade inscriptions such as a label showing manufacturer (902(7)); acknowledged documents (902(8)); commercial paper and related documents (902(9)); and certified domestic records of a regularly conducted activity (902(11)), or foreign ones (902(12)), which let a custodian's declaration replace live testimony. The 2017 amendments added 902(13), for records generated by an electronic process or system, and 902(14), for data copied from an electronic device, storage medium or file, each authenticated by a certification of a qualified person, using process of digital identification for 902(14). Self-authentication of a record does not make it admissible: the hearsay, relevance and other objections remain. Notice requirements usually apply to certifications under 902(11) to (14).

Worked example. The plaintiff offers a printout of a text message in which the defendant says, "I will pay on Friday." The plaintiff testifies that she received it on the number she had always used for the defendant, that it appeared under his name in her phone, and that he later came by with a partial payment on Friday. That supports a finding of authenticity under 901(b)(1) and (b)(4). The defendant may still testify his phone was stolen, a question for the jury. The message also has to clear hearsay, which it does as an opposing party's statement.

lessons.title: The Best Evidence Rule and Summaries
body: The best evidence rule is poorly named. Under Rule 1002, an original writing, recording or photograph is required in order to prove its content, unless the Rules or a federal statute provide otherwise. Two points to keep straight: the rule applies only when a party is trying to prove what a writing, recording or photograph says (its content), and it does not apply simply because a document exists. A witness may testify that she saw a contract signed, or that a person was paid, without producing the document, because she is proving the event, not the content. If the witness is asked what the contract says, the rule applies. The rule also reaches the case where a witness testifies from a document and her testimony essentially recites the document, and courts split on the edge cases such as testimony based on personal knowledge versus a recording of the same event.

Definitions come from Rule 1001. A writing consists of letters, words, numbers or their equivalent set down in any form; a recording is the same kind of material set down by any means; a photograph is a photographic image or its equivalent stored in any form. An original is the writing or recording itself or any counterpart intended to have the same effect by the person who executed or issued it; for electronically stored information, an original includes any printout or other output readable by sight if it accurately reflects the information. A duplicate is a counterpart produced by a mechanical, photographic, chemical, electronic or other process that accurately reproduces the original.

Rule 1003 makes a duplicate admissible to the same extent as the original unless a genuine question is raised about the original's authenticity or the circumstances make it unfair to admit the duplicate. Rule 1004 allows other evidence of content when the original is lost or destroyed (unless the proponent lost or destroyed it in bad faith), when the original cannot be obtained by any available judicial process, when the opponent had control of the original and was notified it would be a subject of proof but failed to produce it, or when the writing is not closely related to a controlling issue. Rule 1005 permits certified copies of public records. Rule 1006 allows a proponent to use a summary, chart or calculation to prove the content of voluminous writings, recordings or photographs that cannot be conveniently examined in court, provided the originals or duplicates are made available for examination or copying at a reasonable time and place; the court may order production. Rule 1007 allows content to be proved by the testimony or written statement of the party against whom it is offered, without accounting for the original. Rule 1008 splits roles between judge and jury: the court decides preliminary admissibility questions such as whether the original was lost, but when an issue is whether an asserted writing ever existed, whether another writing is the original, or whether other evidence of content accurately reflects it, the jury decides.
Distinguish Rule 1006 summaries from Rule 611(a) pedagogical aids, which illustrate evidence already admitted and are not themselves evidence.

Worked example. In a tax dispute, the government wants to prove the content of 40,000 bank transactions. A forensic accountant's spreadsheet summarizing them is admissible under 1006 if the underlying records are admissible and made available to the defense. A witness who says she saw the defendant sign a lease needs no original because she is testifying to the signing, not to the lease terms.

lessons.title: Competency, Personal Knowledge and the Examination of Witnesses
body: The Federal Rules adopt a liberal view of who may testify. Rule 601 says every person is competent to be a witness unless the Rules provide otherwise, and in a civil case, state law governs the witness's competence regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision. Gone are the old disqualifications for felons, spouses, interested parties and the like; concerns of that kind go to credibility. A very young child or a person with a mental disability may testify if she can perceive, remember and relate, and understands the duty to tell the truth, and the judge decides this as a preliminary question.

Rule 602 requires personal knowledge: a witness may testify to a matter only if evidence is introduced sufficient to support a finding that she has personal knowledge of it. This does not apply to an expert's opinion testimony (Rule 703). Rule 603 requires an oath or affirmation to testify truthfully. Rule 604 governs interpreters, who must be qualified and give an oath to translate accurately.

Rule 605 provides that the presiding judge may not testify as a witness at the trial, and no objection is needed to preserve the point. Rule 606 addresses jurors. Under 606(a), a juror may not testify as a witness before the other jurors in the trial, and if a juror is called, the court must give the opposing party an opportunity to object outside the jury's presence. Under 606(b), during an inquiry into the validity of a verdict, a juror may not testify about statements made or incidents that occurred during deliberations, the effect of anything on a juror's or another juror's vote, or a juror's mental processes. There are three exceptions: a juror may testify about whether extraneous prejudicial information was improperly brought to the jury's attention, whether an outside influence was improperly brought to bear on any juror, or whether a mistake was made in entering the verdict on the verdict form. Tanner v. United States (1987) held that juror intoxication during trial is not an outside influence, so the rule barred testimony on it. In Pena-Rodriguez v. Colorado (2017), the Supreme Court recognized a constitutional exception: where a juror makes a clear statement that indicates he or she relied on racial stereotypes or animus to convict a criminal defendant, the no-impeachment rule gives way to permit the trial court to consider the evidence.

Rule 611 gives the court reasonable control over the mode and order of examining witnesses. Cross-examination should not go beyond the subject matter of direct and matters affecting credibility, though the court may allow inquiry into additional matters as if on direct (the federal approach; a number of states follow a wide-open cross rule). Leading questions should not be used on direct except as necessary to develop the testimony, and ordinarily are allowed on cross; the court may allow leading questions of a hostile witness, an adverse party, or a witness identified with an adverse party. Rule 612 lets a witness use a writing to refresh memory, and if she used it while testifying, the adverse party is entitled to have it produced, to inspect it, to cross-examine on it, and to introduce relevant portions in evidence; the court has discretion if she used it before testifying. Rule 615 lets the court, on request, exclude witnesses so that they cannot hear other witnesses' testimony, but not a party who is a natural person, an officer or employee designated as the entity's representative, a person whose presence is essential to the claim, or a person authorized by statute to be present.

Worked example. A witness cannot remember the license plate she saw. Counsel hands her a note she wrote at the scene and asks whether it refreshes her memory. The note is not offered as evidence; she then testifies from her renewed memory. Opposing counsel may inspect the note and cross-examine on it. If instead she cannot recall even after seeing the note, counsel may attempt to lay a foundation for recorded recollection under 803(5), so that it may be read to the jury.

lessons.title: Impeachment: Prior Inconsistent Statements, Bias, Convictions and Truthfulness
body: Impeachment is the attack on a witness's credibility. Under Rule 607, any party, including the one who called the witness, may attack credibility. A party may not use this to call a witness she knows will say nothing helpful merely to introduce otherwise inadmissible prior statements under the guise of impeachment, a limit courts apply to prevent subterfuge. The principal methods follow.

Prior inconsistent statements (Rule 613). Extrinsic evidence of a prior inconsistent statement is admissible only if the witness is given an opportunity to explain or deny the statement and an adverse party is given an opportunity to examine her about it, or if justice so requires. The rule does not require that the statement be shown to the witness before she is asked about it, though on request it must be disclosed to opposing counsel. The extrinsic-evidence requirement does not apply to an opposing party's statement under 801(d)(2). Unless the statement qualifies under 801(d)(1)(A), it is used only to impeach and not for its truth. Courts disallow impeachment on collateral matters by extrinsic evidence, so a witness's answer on a collateral point binds the examiner. Bias, interest and motive are never collateral. Under United States v. Abel (1984), a witness's membership in a secret prison gang with the defendant was properly used to show bias, and the Rules, though silent on bias, permit it.

Character for truthfulness (Rule 608). Under 608(a), a witness's credibility may be attacked or supported by reputation or opinion testimony about her character for truthfulness or untruthfulness, but evidence of truthful character is admissible only after her character for truthfulness has been attacked. Under 608(b), specific instances of conduct may be inquired into on cross-examination if probative of the character for truthfulness or untruthfulness of the witness or of another witness whose character she is testifying about, but extrinsic evidence is not admissible to prove them. By testifying on another matter, a witness does not waive her privilege against self-incrimination for testimony that relates only to her character for truthfulness. Convictions are governed by 609, not 608(b).

Criminal convictions (Rule 609). Under 609(a)(1), a crime punishable by death or imprisonment for more than one year must be admitted in a civil case or in a criminal case where the witness is not a defendant, subject to Rule 403, and in a criminal case where the witness is a defendant, only if the probative value outweighs the prejudicial effect to that defendant. Under 609(a)(2), any crime, regardless of punishment, must be admitted if the court can readily determine that establishing the elements required proving, or the witness admitting, a dishonest act or false statement; there is no balancing. Examples are perjury, fraud and false statement offenses, while theft crimes usually do not qualify absent proof of deceit. A conviction more than ten years old, counting from the conviction or release from confinement, whichever is later, is admissible only if its probative value substantially outweighs its prejudicial effect and the proponent gives reasonable written notice (609(b)). Pardons based on innocence and certain rehabilitation certificates can remove a conviction (609(c)), and juvenile adjudications are generally not admissible, with a narrow exception in criminal cases for witnesses other than the defendant (609(d)). Under Luce v. United States (1984), a defendant who does not testify cannot claim on appeal that an in limine ruling allowing impeachment by a prior

conviction was error, since the reviewing court cannot assess the harm, and Ohler v. United States (2000) held that a defendant who introduces her own conviction on direct cannot appeal the ruling either.

Other rules. Rule 610 bars evidence of religious beliefs or opinions to attack or support credibility on the ground that they affect it. Contradiction by other evidence, capacity impeachment (poor eyesight or intoxication at the time), and rehabilitation by prior consistent statements under 801(d)(1)(B) round out the toolbox.

Worked example. D testifies at his own trial for check fraud. The prosecutor asks about a conviction nine years ago for forging a check. It is a crimen falsi offense, so 609(a)(2) requires admission without balancing. If D had a conviction for aggravated assault, a felony, the court would balance under 609(a)(1)(B), asking whether probative value outweighs prejudice to D.

lessons.title: Lay Opinion, Expert Testimony and the Bases of Opinion
body: The Rules distinguish lay opinion from expert opinion. Under Rule 701, a lay witness's opinion testimony is limited to one that is (a) rationally based on the witness's perception, (b) helpful to clearly understanding the witness's testimony or to determining a fact in issue, and (c) not based on scientific, technical or other specialized knowledge within the scope of Rule 702. Familiar examples include a witness's estimate of speed or distance, that a person appeared intoxicated or angry, the identity of a voice, handwriting familiarity, and the value of one's own property. The third prong, added in 2000, prevents a party from sidestepping the reliability gate and the disclosure requirements of Rule 702 and the civil and criminal discovery rules by offering an expert's opinion through a lay witness. A police officer who saw a transaction can describe it, but opinions about drug-dealer codes that rest on training typically require expert qualification.

Rule 702 governs experts. A witness who is qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training or education may testify in the form of an opinion or otherwise if the proponent demonstrates to the court that it is more likely than not that (a) the expert's scientific, technical or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) the expert's opinion reflects a reliable application of the principles and methods to the facts of the case. The "more likely than not" language comes from a December 2023 amendment meant to correct decisions that treated sufficiency of basis and application as matters of weight for the jury; the court acts as gatekeeper on all of (a) to (d). An expert may be qualified by experience alone, and the question is qualification on the specific subject. Rule 706 lets the court appoint its own expert.

Rule 703 on the bases of an expert's opinion. An expert may base an opinion on facts or data in the case that the expert has been made aware of or personally observed. If experts in the field would reasonably rely on those kinds of facts or data in forming an opinion, they need not be admissible for the opinion to be admitted. But if the facts or data would otherwise be inadmissible, the proponent may disclose them to the jury only if their probative value in helping the jury evaluate the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect. This weighted test is the reverse of Rule 403, tilted against disclosure. A limiting instruction is typically given because the basis evidence is not admitted for its truth (and see the Confrontation Clause discussion in the earlier track). A physician may rely on a patient's history and test results by others.

Rule 704(a) says an opinion is not objectionable just because it embraces an ultimate issue, abolishing the old ultimate-issue rule. But opinions that merely tell the jury what result to reach or that state legal conclusions are excluded as unhelpful under Rules 701 and 702. Rule 704(b), in a criminal case, forbids an expert witness from stating an opinion about whether the defendant did or did not have a mental state or condition that constitutes an element of the crime charged or of a defense; those are for the trier of fact. An expert may describe a defendant's diagnosis and its characteristics, but may not say that the defendant did or did not "intend to kill." Rule 705 allows an expert to state an opinion and give reasons without first testifying to the underlying facts or data, unless the court requires otherwise, and the expert may be required to disclose them on cross-examination.

Worked example. At a robbery trial, a bystander testifies that the robber "was very nervous" and "ran about as fast as a car on a side street." Both are rationally based lay opinions. An officer who testifies that the chalk-like substance in the robber's bag was a certain drug, on the basis of training in drug identification, is giving expert testimony and must qualify under 702.

lessons.title: The Daubert Gatekeeping Standard
body: Before 1993, the leading test for admitting novel scientific evidence in many courts was Frye v. United States (D.C. Cir. 1923): the technique must have gained general acceptance in the relevant scientific community. In Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (1993), the Supreme Court held that the Federal Rules of Evidence, particularly Rule 702, superseded Frye in federal courts. The trial judge must act as a gatekeeper, ensuring that expert testimony rests on a reliable foundation and is relevant to the task at hand. Daubert's case involved the drug Bendectin and claims of birth defects. The Court gave a flexible, non-exclusive list of factors: whether the theory or technique can be (and has been) tested; whether it has been subjected to peer review and publication; the known or potential rate of error and the existence of standards controlling its operation; and general acceptance, which remains a relevant factor though not a precondition. The inquiry focuses on principles and methodology, not on the conclusions they generate.

General Electric Co. v. Joiner (1997) held that appellate courts review a trial court's Daubert decision for abuse of discretion, including a decision to exclude. It also held that conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct: a court may conclude there is simply too great an analytical gap between the data and the opinion proffered, and need not admit evidence connected to the data only by the ipse dixit of the expert. In Kumho Tire Co. v. Carmichael (1999), the Court held that the gatekeeping obligation applies to all expert testimony, including technical and other specialized knowledge such as the opinion of a tire-failure engineer, not only to "scientific" testimony. The Daubert factors may be applied where reasonable, but the judge has broad latitude in deciding how to test reliability, and may use other factors suited to the field.

Rule 702 was amended in 2000 to codify these cases, and again effective December 1, 2023, to make clear that the proponent must demonstrate to the court that it is more likely than not that the admissibility requirements are met, and that the expert's opinion must stay within the bounds of what can be concluded from a reliable application of the method. The Advisory Committee noted that many courts had wrongly held that questions of sufficiency of the basis and application of the method were for the jury; those questions are admissibility issues under Rule 104(a). As of this writing, courts are still applying the amendment, and decisions vary in how strictly they enforce it.

A number of states retain the Frye standard (a few of the large ones, including California, Illinois, New York and Pennsylvania, did when last checked), while many others follow Daubert or a variant; the split should be named, not assumed. Gatekeeping applies at a pretrial hearing or in limine; the court can decide on papers, and failure to hold a hearing is not necessarily error. Shaky but admissible evidence is attacked by vigorous cross-examination and contrary evidence, as Daubert noted.

Worked example. A plaintiff's expert testifies that a chemical caused her illness, relying on animal studies at very high doses and anecdotal case reports, and offers no epidemiological data or reasoning to bridge the gap. The defendant moves to exclude. Under Joiner, the court may find an analytical gap too wide between the data and the opinion, and exclude the testimony under Rule 702(b) to (d). The ruling will be reviewed only for abuse of discretion.

lessons.title: Privilege Basics and the Attorney-Client Privilege
body: A privilege lets a holder refuse to disclose, and prevent others from disclosing, certain information even though it is relevant and reliable. Privileges exclude otherwise good evidence to protect relationships or interests that society values, so courts construe them narrowly. Federal Rule of Evidence 501 does not codify privileges. It says that the common law, as interpreted by United States courts in the light of reason and experience, governs a claim of privilege unless the Constitution, a federal statute or rules prescribed by the Supreme Court provide otherwise; but in a civil case, state law governs privilege regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision. Thus in a federal diversity case, state privilege law applies, while in a federal-question case or a federal criminal case, federal common law applies. The Rules also leave out the privilege rules the Advisory Committee originally proposed.

The attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications between client and lawyer made for the purpose of obtaining or providing legal advice. The classic elements are: a communication, made in confidence, between a client (or prospective client) and a lawyer or the lawyer's agent, for the purpose of seeking or giving legal advice. The privilege protects the communication, not the underlying facts: a client may not hide a fact (what she saw or did) by telling it to a lawyer, though she cannot be forced to reveal what she told the lawyer. Presence of a third party generally destroys confidentiality, except for those necessary to the consultation, such as a lawyer's assistant or an interpreter. The privilege belongs to the client, who can waive it.

Upjohn Co. v. United States (1981) rejected the narrow "control group" test for corporate clients. The Court held that communications from lower-level employees to corporate counsel, made at the direction of superiors to secure legal advice about matters within the employees' duties, are privileged. The privilege belongs to the corporation. In Swidler & Berlin v. United States (1998), the Court held that the privilege survives the client's death, at least in the criminal context, and may not be overridden by a prosecutor's showing of need. There are recognized exceptions to the privilege: the crime-fraud exception (communications made in furtherance of a continuing or future crime or fraud, not those regarding past wrongdoing), disputes between joint clients, a dispute between lawyer and client (such as fee disputes or malpractice), and certain testamentary disputes among persons claiming through the same deceased client.

Rule 502 addresses waiver. Under 502(a), a disclosure made in a federal proceeding or to a federal office or agency waives the privilege or work-product protection as to undisclosed material only if the waiver is intentional, the disclosed and undisclosed communications concern the same subject matter, and they ought in fairness to be considered together. Under 502(b), inadvertent disclosure does not waive if the holder took reasonable steps to prevent disclosure and promptly took reasonable steps to rectify the error. Under 502(d), a federal court may order that the privilege or protection is not waived by disclosure connected with the litigation pending before it, and the order binds other federal and state proceedings; this is the basis of "clawback" agreements.

The work-product doctrine, from Hickman v. Taylor (1947) and now Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(b)(3), is not a privilege in the strict sense but a qualified immunity from discovery for materials prepared in anticipation of litigation by or for a party or its representative. Ordinary work product can be discovered on a showing of substantial need and inability to obtain the equivalent without undue hardship, while opinion work product (the mental impressions, conclusions and legal theories of counsel) is nearly absolutely protected.

Worked example. A company's in-house lawyer interviews a mid-level manager about a possible regulatory violation, so as to advise the company. The conversation is privileged under Upjohn. If the manager tells a friend what she said to the lawyer, the friend may be compelled to testify, as the manager's disclosure is not the company's. If the company used the lawyer to plan a fraud, the crime-fraud exception defeats the privilege for those communications.

lessons.title: Spousal, Psychotherapist, Self-Incrimination and Other Privileges
body: Beyond attorney-client communications, the main privileges tested in evidence courses are the two spousal privileges, the psychotherapist-patient privilege, and the privilege against self-incrimination. Because Rule 501 leaves them to common-law development in federal court, and states differ, the examiner will usually say which law governs.

Spousal privileges come in two forms. The spousal testimonial privilege (spousal immunity) lets a witness-spouse decline to testify adversely against her spouse in a criminal case. In Trammel v. United States (1980), the Supreme Court held that under federal law the privilege belongs to the witness-spouse alone, who may choose to testify or not, and the defendant-spouse cannot block her testimony. The privilege generally lasts only during the marriage. The confidential marital communications privilege protects confidential communications made between spouses during a valid marriage. It covers communications, not acts or observations, and it survives the end of the marriage as to communications made during it. Under the usual federal approach, either spouse can assert the privilege to block disclosure of confidential communications, and it applies in civil and criminal cases. Common exceptions include proceedings in which the spouses are adverse, crimes against one another or against a child of either, and, in many courts, communications made in furtherance of joint criminal activity. Presence of a third party defeats confidentiality. State laws vary on both spousal privileges, so "majority rule" claims should be made cautiously.

In Jaffee v. Redmond (1996), the Supreme Court recognized under Rule 501 a federal psychotherapist-patient privilege covering confidential communications made to licensed psychotherapists, including licensed clinical social workers, during diagnosis or treatment. Balancing tests case by case were rejected, because a privilege that is uncertain in application does not serve its purpose. The Court left open the contours of exceptions, such as a patient's dangerousness to others, which some lower courts have recognized. There is no general federal physician-patient privilege, though many states have created one by statute. Statutory privileges for clergy-penitent communications exist in all states, with varying scopes, and a federal common-law privilege for confessions to clergy is generally accepted.

The Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination protects a person from being compelled to be a witness against herself in a criminal case, and extends to testimony in any proceeding where the answers might incriminate her in a later one. It is personal, so a witness cannot assert it for another, and a corporation has no Fifth Amendment privilege. A criminal defendant has an absolute right not to testify, and the prosecution may not comment on silence at trial, as Griffin v. California (1965) held. A witness other than the accused must invoke the privilege question by question (a blanket assertion is generally not enough), and the judge decides whether the answer would have a tendency to incriminate. Testimony may be compelled if the government grants immunity that is at least as broad as the privilege (use and derivative-use immunity). The act-of-production doctrine can protect a person who would, by producing documents, authenticate or acknowledge their existence.

A privilege is generally waived by voluntary disclosure of a significant part of the communication, and the holder is the one who can waive it. Some privilege disputes arise over the "at issue" waiver: a party that puts a privileged communication at issue cannot use it as a sword while hiding it as a shield.

Worked example. Pat is charged with fraud. Pat's spouse Ana saw Pat count cash at home, and Pat told Ana privately that the cash came from the scheme. Under federal law, Ana alone decides whether to testify against Pat (Trammel). Pat's private statement to Ana is a confidential marital communication that Pat can block her from revealing, unless a recognized exception such as joint criminal activity applies; what Ana saw (the cash) is not a communication.

lessons.title: Burdens of Proof and Presumptions
body: Burdens have two parts. The burden of production (also called the burden of going forward) requires a party to produce enough evidence on an issue to avoid an adverse ruling such as a directed verdict or judgment as a matter of law. The burden of persuasion requires a party to convince the factfinder to the required degree. In most civil cases the standard is preponderance of the evidence, meaning more likely than not. Some civil issues require clear and convincing evidence (fraud, certain wills or termination of parental rights), which is a higher but not criminal level. In criminal cases, due process requires the prosecution to prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt (In re Winship, 1970). The allocation of burdens is substantive in nature, and the burden of persuasion generally rests on the party who asserts a claim or affirmative defense. The burden of production can shift back and forth during a trial, but the burden of persuasion generally does not.

Presumptions are devices that require the factfinder to find a presumed fact once a basic fact is established, unless rebutted. Rule 301 governs civil cases in federal court: unless a federal statute or the Rules provide otherwise, the party against whom a presumption is directed has the burden of producing evidence to rebut the presumption, but the rule does not shift the burden of persuasion, which remains on the party who had it originally. This is the Thayer or "bursting bubble" approach: once enough evidence to rebut is produced, the presumption has done its job and the factfinder decides the issue on the evidence. Many states follow the Morgan approach for some presumptions, where the presumption shifts the burden of persuasion to the opponent; this is a state-law split that should be named, not assumed. Rule 302 provides that in a civil case, state law governs the effect of a presumption regarding a claim or defense for which state law supplies the rule of decision. Familiar presumptions include the presumption that a properly mailed letter was received (the mailbox rule), the presumption of legitimacy of a child born to a married woman, and the presumption of death after seven years' unexplained absence in many jurisdictions. Some presumptions are conclusive, which is really a substantive rule of law rather than evidence law.

Presumptions against criminal defendants face constitutional limits. A mandatory presumption (the jury must find the elemental fact) that relieves the prosecution of its burden on an element violates due process. In Sandstrom v. Montana (1979), an instruction that "the law presumes that a person intends the ordinary consequences of his voluntary acts" was held unconstitutional because a jury could have read it as conclusive or as shifting the burden on intent. A permissive inference, one the jury may but need not draw, is permitted if there is a rational connection between the basic fact and the inferred fact, and as applied beyond a reasonable doubt where it is the sole basis for conviction, as County Court of Ulster County v. Allen (1979) held for a statutory inference from presence of a firearm in a car. Patterson v. New York (1977) held that a state may place on the defendant the burden of proving an affirmative defense such as extreme emotional disturbance, so long as the prosecution still proves each element of the offense beyond a reasonable doubt.

Worked example. A statute provides that a letter properly addressed and mailed is presumed received. The sender proves mailing; the recipient testifies that he never received it. Under Rule 301, the burden of production shifted to the recipient, who met it by testifying, so the presumption disappears and the jury decides receipt on all the evidence, though the jury may still draw the inference from the mailing evidence, and the sender keeps the burden of persuasion.

lessons.title: Judicial Notice
body: Judicial notice is the court's acceptance of a fact as true without requiring formal evidence. Rule 201 governs only adjudicative facts, which are the facts of the particular case, such as who did what, when and where. Legislative facts, the general facts a court uses in making law or policy, such as empirical premises behind a rule, are not governed by Rule 201, and judges use them freely, as they do the law itself, which the court knows or finds on its own (for foreign law, Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 44.1 applies).

Under Rule 201(b), a court may judicially notice a fact that is not subject to reasonable dispute because it (1) is generally known within the trial court's territorial jurisdiction, or (2) can be accurately and readily determined from sources whose accuracy cannot reasonably be questioned. Examples of the first type are that a major local street runs north-south or that a particular city is on a particular river. Examples of the second are the day of the week on which a calendar date fell, the distance between two cities from a standard atlas, a court's own records, and official government data such as weather reports from the National Weather Service. Courts take notice that a document was filed in another case but, usually, do not take notice of the truth of contested statements inside it, and noticing a fact such as a company's stock price on a given day is acceptable from a reliable source. A judge's personal knowledge gained outside the courtroom does not qualify by itself.

Procedure. The court may take judicial notice on its own, and must take it if a party requests and supplies the court with the necessary information (201(c)). On timely request, a party is entitled to be heard on the propriety of taking judicial notice and on the nature of the fact to be noticed; if the court takes notice before notifying a party, the party, on request, is still entitled to be heard afterward (201(e)). The court may take judicial notice at any stage of the proceeding (201(d)), including on appeal, though appellate courts do so cautiously.

Effect on the jury. In a civil case, the court must instruct the jury to accept the noticed fact as conclusive. In a criminal case, the court must instruct the jury that it may or may not accept the noticed fact as conclusive (201(f)). The criminal-case rule preserves the defendant's right to a jury determination of every element, which the Sixth Amendment protects; a directed finding on an element against the accused would violate it. Therefore noticed facts in a criminal case are, in effect, permissive.

Traps. A fact that is generally known but disputed is not appropriate for notice. Notice cannot be used to establish a fact that depends on the credibility of a source, such as a newspaper's account of an event. A court may notice that a website exists or what it said on a date through an archive, but not that its content is true. Courts differ on how far they go with information found by search engines, and the examiner will often add an adjective such as "reputable" to signal the answer.

Worked example. In a contract dispute, the plaintiff says the defendant's notice was sent on a Sunday, which would affect a deadline. The court may notice that the date fell on a Sunday from a calendar. In a criminal trial for a crime committed in a county, the court may notice that the county lies within the district, but will tell the jury that it may, rather than must, accept the fact.

questions.prompt: Under Federal Rule of Evidence 401, evidence is relevant if it:
choices: is likely to change the outcome of the case in the opinion of the presiding judge
is reliable enough that it would be admitted under an established hearsay exception
has any tendency to make a fact of consequence more or less probable than it would be without the evidence
is sufficient on its own to prove an element of the claim or defense by a preponderance of the evidence presented at trial

questions.prompt: In an injury suit, the plaintiff offers a letter the defendant allegedly received warning of a hazard. Receipt is disputed. Which description of the judge's role is most accurate?
choices: Under Rule 105, the judge must instruct the jury to disregard the letter unless the defendant admits that it was received
Under Rule 403, the judge must exclude the letter whenever the defendant disputes receipt because the dispute creates unfair prejudice
Under Rule 104(a), the judge must find by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant received the letter before the jury may be allowed to hear it at all
Under Rule 104(b), the judge asks only whether a reasonable jury could find the defendant received the letter, and lets the jury decide receipt

questions.prompt: In a joint trial, a statement is admissible against one defendant but not against the other, and the second defendant's lawyer wants to limit its use. What does Rule 105 provide?
choices: On request, the court must restrict the evidence to its proper scope and instruct the jury accordingly

What is the best ruling?

Rule 105 forbids any limiting instruction in a joint criminal trial because jurors cannot be presumed to follow it

questions.prompt: Under Rule 403, a court may exclude relevant evidence if its probative value is:

less than the probative value of other available evidence that proves the same fact in a different, equally convincing way
merely equal to the danger of unfair prejudice that the evidence presents to the opposing party

Admit all of them because the prosecution has an absolute right to choose the form of its proof without any judicial limits

questions.prompt: In Old Chief v. United States (1997), the Supreme Court held that the trial court abused its discretion when it:

refused the defendant's offer to stipulate to his felon status and allowed the prosecution to prove the name and nature of the prior offense

Rule 104(a), because the court must exclude any evidence whose foundation cannot be established by a witness with personal knowledge

when offered by a criminal defendant to prove his own good character through any witness
for any purpose, including impeachment of witnesses and proof of an essential element of a claim
unless the judge finds that the evidence is more probative than prejudicial on the issue of the actor's identity or motive

questions.prompt: D is on trial for assault. He calls a neighbor who says D has a reputation as a peaceful person. May the prosecutor cross-examine the neighbor about D's earlier barroom fight?

Admissible because Rule 407 applies only to measures taken by someone other than the defendant

questions.prompt: Gina sues Hal Corp., her employer, for a workplace injury. Hal Corp. denies it owns the machine, saying a contractor does. Exclude it entirely because Rule 407 bars subsequent measures for every purpose, including ownership

Inadmissible under Rule 410 because the statement was made during plea discussions with a prosecuting attorney that did not result in a guilty plea

to prove that the declarant had a motive to speak the words that were spoken
to prove the truth of the matter asserted in the statement
to show that the statement was made by someone with personal knowledge

made in a signed writing that the witness acknowledged at any time in the presence of a police officer

only when the item is more than twenty years old and offered under the ancient documents exception

whenever any party mentions that such an item exists, even if its content is not in dispute

questions.prompt: A witness testifies that she watched the defendant sign a lease. She is not asked about the terms of the lease. The defense objects that the original lease was not produced. The best ruling is:
choices: Sustain; any testimony about a signed document requires the original under the best evidence rule, even testimony about the act of signing
Overrule only if the original has been destroyed in a fire without the proponent's bad faith
Sustain; testimony about a contract is always hearsay if the contract itself is not in evidence
Overrule; she is proving the event of signing from personal knowledge, not the content of the lease

questions.prompt: Under Rule 1003, a duplicate is admissible to the same extent as the original unless:
